rashi:a1.1: A flaw of placing hands: For until Yosef ben Yo’ezer they did not disagree about placing hands, nor about anything at all, since the heart had not yet been diminished. And it mentions placing hands because that was the first dispute in which the Sages ever disagreed. And from Yosef ben Yo’ezer onward there was among them the flaw of placing hands, for they disagreed about placing hands on peace offerings on a Festival, as we say in Ḥagiga (16a): Shammai says to place hands, and Hillel says not to place hands. [In the mishna in Ḥagiga, Shammai says not to place hands and Hillel says to place hands.]
rashi:a2.1: But Yosef himself disputed: about it, in tractate Ḥagiga (there).
rashi:a2.2: When the heart was limited: for the heart was diminished at the end of his years, [and things] were forgotten.
rashi:a4.1: Was forgotten during the days of mourning for Moses: whether it dies or grazes; and it is one of those halakhot. [Mnemonic:] Y-A-P-Sh: Joshua asked first, after him Samuel, after him Pinehas, after him Elazar. [Mnemonic:] Y-A-P-Sh: Joshua, Elazar, Pinehas, Samuel. [Mnemonic:] Y-P-L-L: Joshua, Pinehas, Elazar, Samuel. [These are mnemonics for different versions of the order in which the four were asked; as printed, the letters do not all match the names given.]
rashi:a6.1: And were forgotten by him: by Joshua, as a punishment for having caused Moses’ mind to be weakened, for Moses was pained by Joshua, [who spoke as if] he himself were as great as [Moses].
rashi:a6.2: To kill him: unless he would tell them [the halakhot].
rashi:a8.1: A fortiori inferences: expositions by a fortiori reasoning.
rashi:a8.2: Minutiae of the scribes: It is explained in Shekalim (chapter 5, halakha 1 [of the Jerusalem Talmud]) that they made the Torah into counts upon counts, for example: fifteen women exempt their rival wives [from levirate marriage]; thirteen things were said about the carcass of a kosher bird; five may not separate teruma. For they joined the matters together and counted them as one, so that they would not be forgotten. And of those minutiae that they had not yet joined together, [some] were forgotten during the days of mourning for Moses.
rashi:a9.1: And Othniel took it: Kiriath Sefer. And what is Kiriath Sefer? Halakhot.
rashi:a9.2: Angry at his wife: because of her [Achsah’s] beauty.
rashi:a10.1: Vatitznaḥ: a term of shouting; she cries out.
rashi:a11.1: Dried [menugav]: desolate and dry of all good.
rashi:a11.2: [Other than Torah alone: for the Torah is called water.] And Othniel was not wealthy, but wise.
rashi:a11.3: Springs [gullot] of water: the Torah; that is, a man to whom the Torah is revealed [geluya].
rashi:a11.4: Request sustenance from him: for this one will certainly not need it, as it is written about her [the woman of valor] (Proverbs 31:14): “She is like the merchant ships,” etc.
rashi:a12.1: Son of Kenaz: For it is written above, “Othniel, son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb,” which implies that Caleb was the son of Kenaz; for it is written elsewhere (Joshua 14:6), “Caleb, son of Jephunneh, the Kenizzite,” and it is not written “son of Kenaz.”
rashi:a13.1: Begot Azubah, [his] wife: It is explained in the first chapter of Sota (12a) that he married Miriam, who was abandoned [azuva] because of illness; and since he married her for the sake of Heaven, the verse regards him as though he had begotten her.
rashi:a13.2: The stepson of Kenaz: and Othniel was his brother from the mother.
rashi:a13.3: This is also precise: that Caleb was not the son of Kenaz, for it is written elsewhere, “Caleb, son of Jephunneh, the Kenizzite,” and it is not written “son of Kenaz”; evidently Kenaz raised him but did not beget him. [Rashi’s text here has the words “this is also precise,” which are not in the printed Gemara.]
rashi:a15.1: And that You will work deliverance from evil, that it may not [pain me]: that is, “that it may not”: that the evil inclination should not overpower me from studying; that the evil inclination should not overpower me so that I neglect Torah study.
rashi:a15.2: My pain [otzbi]: implies a term of sorrow [etzev]. And thus he said before Him: If You do this for me, good; and if not, I go in my depression [nesisi] to the netherworld, that is, I die in my sorrow, as we translate [in the Aramaic Targum] (Genesis 34:7) “and they were grieved” as “ve’itnesisu.”
rashi:a17.1: On a similar note you say: that whoever devotes himself to pursuing Torah, his requests are fulfilled for him.
rashi:a17.2: And the oppressor [ish tekhakhim]: a middling [scholar], who knows two or three orders [of the Mishna], who is of middling standing.
rashi:a17.3: Gives light to the eyes of both of them: for the teacher too still needs learning, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, teaches him.
rashi:a17.4: The maker of them all: now He begins to make them anew, this one wise and that one foolish.
rashi:a19.1: On a similar note, etc.: that one who asks for his sustenance and his needs, Heaven attends to him to fulfill his requests.
rashi:a24.1: Unspecified: [the sin offering] whose owner achieved atonement, and [the one] whose year has passed.
rashi:a24.2: Specified: the offspring, its substitute, and one whose owner died, for which it is specified to us that they do not occur in a community.
rashi:b1.1: But can one derive the possible from the impossible: the reason these three are not [included] in a community for death is because they are not found in a community at all, neither with regard to death nor with regard to sacrifice, for they never occur in a community.
rashi:b2.1: Four were given to them: All of them, four sin offerings, were given to them from Sinai as dying, and not five (either in an individual or in a community, and they forgot of which it was said to them that it dies); and of the fifth it was said to them that it grazes. And in the days of mourning for Moses they forgot which one grazes, and they went stringently and said: All of them die. Therefore, if it enters your mind that it was said to them of a community, are they found in a community? Only two of them occur in a community. Rather, it is certainly only of an individual.
rashi:b3.1: One was given to them: for death, and four for grazing; and they established it as five, since they forgot which one dies. And Rabbi Natan comes to explain the reason of Rabbi Shimon in the mishna, but before he concludes his statement the Gemara challenges him and answers its challenge, and then he concludes his statement.
rashi:b4.1: But let them see in which category they learned it: Why did they establish it as five because of an uncertainty about one? Let them see in which category they learned that one. If they remembered that the one that dies, which was said to them, could occur both in an individual and in a community, they would learn that a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement and one whose year has passed die out of uncertainty; but about those three there is no uncertainty, since they do not occur in a community and are not similar to that one. And if they remembered that the one that dies could occur only in an individual, let them say that those three die; but here [with the other two] there is no uncertainty, since they are not similar to it.
rashi:b5.1: They forgot two things: from which category, and which one it is. And therefore, since they forgot everything, it was difficult for those in the days of Joshua: If it enters your mind that the one that dies was [said] of a community, the four that graze, how would you find them in a community? They never occur there. Rather, certainly, since five were mentioned, between death and grazing, it was said of an individual, in whom all of them are found. And this is the reason of Rabbi Shimon. And the Rabbis hold: Four were given to them [to die] wherever we find them: where it exists both in an individual and in a community, it exists; where it does not exist in a community, it does not. And elsewhere my teacher explained it thus: Reish Lakish said: It is not a matter of reasoning but a received tradition, that four were given to them for death in one statement. And since they were taught together in one tradition, certainly they taught the four in one context, and one does not find four except in an individual. “And they established them as five”: the fifth was given to them for grazing, and they decreed death upon it stringently, out of uncertainty, since they forgot which one it is; and it was forgotten in the days of mourning for Moses. “And it was difficult for them,” etc.: for those in the days of Joshua. If it enters your mind that they were taught of a community: after all, it was one context, since the four were taught in one tradition, and in a community can you find four? Therefore “it dies” was said of an individual and not of a community, and wherever it occurs in a community it grazes, for it is obvious to us that [the death] of sin offerings does not apply in a community. And the reason he says “four were given to them,” etc., is because that is how the event was, for certainly this halakha was forgotten in the days of mourning for Moses; he does not put it this way for the sake of answering [the question on] Rabbi Shimon, for all the more so, if all of them had been given for death, Rabbi Shimon’s statement would be answered even better. “Rabbi Natan says,” etc.: also to answer this [question]. One was given to them for death and four for grazing, and they forgot which one dies, and they established all of them for death. And since the four that graze were learned in one tradition and at one time, certainly they were learned in one context: either all of them of an individual, or all of them of both an individual and a community. Therefore, perforce, in one context you find them only in an individual, and we learn it from the ones that graze. And this is not [deriving] from the impossible, for among those four that graze there is perforce one that can occur in a community, and even so they learned it of an individual, since it was said in one statement. Therefore we learn the fifth, the one that dies, from it: just as this one, which can occur in an individual and in a community, was said only of an individual, so too this one, even if it is one of those that can occur in a community, its death was said only of an individual. Therefore we do derive the possible from the impossible, and we establish death for an individual and not for a community. And what is the case of [deriving] the possible from the impossible that we do not derive? For example, if they had learned three in one tradition for grazing and two in one tradition for death, and wanted to learn these from those: just as the three that graze were said only of an individual, since three are not found in a community, so too the two that die were said only of an individual. There one could refute: Can one derive the possible from the impossible? Perhaps establish those three, which do not occur in a community, for grazing, and those two, which occur here and there, for death wherever they occur. And also when they come to those three that exist only in an individual, there is room for uncertainty: perhaps death was said of an individual, and of two of those three, and grazing of the three others, for all of them are found in an individual. “But let them see in which category they learned it”: why did they establish it as five because of one? Let them see from which category that one was. If the one that dies was from the category of those found in an individual and in a community, there is uncertainty about those two sin offerings, whose owner achieved atonement and whose year has passed; but about the offspring of a sin offering, the substitute, and one whose owner died there is no uncertainty, since it is obvious to us that the one for death was one of those fit to be found in a community. If it was one of the three that are not found in a community, let them establish all three of those for death; but why did they establish [the ones] whose owner achieved atonement and whose year has passed [for death], when it is obvious to them that the one that dies could not be found in a community?
rashi:b5.2: They forgot two things: from which category it was and which one it is; therefore they established all of them for death. “And it was difficult for them”: now he returns to the first answer, and Rabbi Natan concludes his statement to answer Rabbi Shimon’s statement. Until now the Gemara interrupted, challenging his statement about why he said “they established them as five.”
rashi:b7.1: MISHNA: And one consecrates limbs and fetuses, but one does not substitute: This is Rabbi Yehuda, who expounds “an animal for an animal” in the first chapter (above, Temurah 10b).
rashi:b8.1: On one with a permanent blemish: that if one substituted a blemished animal for an unblemished consecrated animal, so severe a sanctity takes effect on it that if it is redeemed it does not go out to non-sacred status.
tosafot:b1.1: In brief: In Horayot (6b) the Gemara answers this question with “they all were learned in one tradition”: all five sin offerings were taught in one series, and since some of them cannot occur in a community, all of them were taught as not applying in a community. Here, Tosafot read: Reish Lakish said: Four were given to them, and they established them as five. That is, at Sinai they were given four that die and one that grazes, and in the days of mourning for Moses they forgot which one, and decreed that all of them die; and if it enters your mind [that the tradition was] of a community, are these found in a community? Rather, perforce, the unspecified is learned from the specified. Tosafot explain the argument step by step. Needless to say, had all five been taught as dying, they would have been taught as one unit, and since some of them do not occur in a community, none of them applies in a community. But even now, when one of them was taught as grazing, we say that none of them applies in a community. If the one that grazes is one of those not found in a community, then the four taught to die were taught in one tradition, and since at least two of them were taught not of a community, the other two were likewise taught not of a community. And even if the one that grazes was [the sin offering] whose owner achieved atonement or whose year had passed, the other of that pair was taught to die together with the three that do not occur in a community, so the fourth too does not apply in a community. And the one that was taught to graze, which they forgot and on which they decreed death: even though it can occur in a community, we derive the possible from the impossible. Since the four were taught to die of an individual and not of a community, as one tradition, the one that was forgotten and on which death was decreed also dies only of an individual and not of a community. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b3.1: Rabbi Natan says: One was given, and they established it as five: That is, at Sinai one that dies and four that graze were given to them, and in the days of mourning for Moses it was forgotten which ones die and which graze; therefore they decreed that all of them die. And he relies on what he concludes: “Just as the specified is of an individual,” etc. But the Gemara challenges his words before we conclude, and then we conclude Rabbi Natan’s statement. And it asks: “But let them see in which category they learned it, whether of a community or of an individual.” That is: why did they decree death on all of them? There are three among them that exist in an individual and not in a community, and two that exist in a community. Let them see: if the one taught to die is from the three, let them decree death on the three, and the two should graze; and if it is from the two, they should have decreed death only on the two, and the three should graze. And it answers: They forgot two things: which one was taught for death, and also whether it was from the two or from the three; therefore they decreed death on all of them. And now he concludes his statement: “And it was difficult for them: If it enters your mind,” etc. “Rather, conclude from it: The unspecified is learned from the specified. Just as the specified,” etc. (That is, one that was taught to graze, and they learned them in one tradition, and the unspecified is learned from the specified.) That is, the four that were taught to graze were taught in one tradition, and the unspecified is learned from the specified, all as we explained with regard to the statement of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.
gershom:a1.1: Rav Yosef said: what it says, “from then on there was a flaw in them,” means a flaw of disputes: that they did not serve [their teachers] as much as was needed, and would disagree with one another’s words. Another version: the flaw of placing hands, that they disagreed about placing hands, as Shammai says (not) to place hands and Hillel says not to place hands. [The text is garbled here; in the mishna in Ḥagiga (16a), Shammai says not to place hands and Hillel says to place hands.]
gershom:a2.1: [When Yosei ben Yo’ezer disagreed,] it was at the end of his years, when the heart was limited by great (troubles) [old age].
gershom:a3.1: They said to Joshua: Ask: through the Divine Spirit, that it explain them to you.
gershom:a4.1: He said to them: It is not in heaven: [the Torah], for it has already been given to us in its entirety. [Mnemonic: Y-Sh-P-A: Joshua, Samuel, Pinehas, Elazar. Some say Y-P-A-Sh: Joshua, Pinehas, Elazar, Samuel. Y-P-L-L: Joshua, Pinehas, Elazar, Samuel.]
gershom:a5.1: Did I ever leave you: that is, I have no uncertainty. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: It is impossible to tell you, for it is not in heaven.
gershom:a6.1: And of the minutiae of the scribes: [the counting of matters], for example: fifteen women exempt [their rival wives]; thirteen things were said about the carcass of a kosher bird. And this is Kiriath Sefer.
gershom:a7.1: Angry at his wife: that his wife seemed ugly to him [compared with her]. [Othniel, son of Kenaz, was Caleb’s brother from his mother, and Caleb was Kenaz’s stepson and was called by his name because he raised him.]
gershom:a8.1: Vatitznaḥ: is (like “and she cried”) [like “and she shouted”].
gershom:a9.1: A man who is dried of all good, of money.
gershom:a10.1: Springs of water: a man in whom there are words of Torah, which are likened to water.
gershom:a11.1: He said to her: Caleb [said]: I gave you a man to whom the secrets of the upper and the lower worlds are revealed [by his great wisdom], and it is not enough for you, and you still request sustenance [from him]? [In my depression] to the netherworld: angry, [to the netherworld,] to the grave, [as in] “and behold, they were troubled [zo’afim]” (Genesis 40:6), which we translate [in the Aramaic Targum] as “nesisin.”
gershom:a12.1: [Immediately: “And God granted him that which he requested.”] On a similar note: “The poor man and the oppressor”: the poor man, this is one poor in Torah.
gershom:a13.1: And the oppressor [ish tekhakhim]: this is one middling in Torah, for example one who knows two orders [of the Mishna]. And when the poor man says to the ish tekhakhim, “Teach me,” he is obligated to teach him and to do his will by teaching him, just as the Holy One, Blessed be He, did the will of Othniel, [answering him,] as it is written: “And God granted him that which he requested.” This is “on a similar note.”
gershom:a14.1: And Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: explains “the poor man and the oppressor” as referring to money; and [the homeowner] is obligated to support him and to do his will, just as the Holy One, Blessed be He, did for Othniel.
gershom:a15.1: And if he does so, “the Lord gives light to the eyes of both of them”: both of them become wealthy.
gershom:a16.1: [Whose owner achieved atonement and whose year has passed: We did not learn that one cannot fulfill them in a community. One might say that in a community they do not die. Learn the unspecified ones, whose owner achieved atonement and whose year has passed, of which we do not know whether they are of a community or of an individual, from the specified: from the offspring of a sin offering, the substitute of a sin offering, and one whose owner died. Just as these are of an individual and not of a community, so too these.]
gershom:b1.1: But can one derive the possible from the impossible: for these two can be fulfilled both in an individual and in a community.
gershom:b2.1: Reish Lakish said: This is why we derive the possible from the impossible: four sin offerings that die were given to them at Mount Sinai, and they did not know which ones, and they established them as five out of uncertainty. And if it enters your mind that they are of a community, (two in general) [that is,] four of these five cannot occur in a community, as we said. Rather, [certainly,] perforce, the unspecified is learned from the specified.
gershom:b3.1: Rabbi Natan says: One was given to them that dies, and they forgot which one is the one that dies, and they established it as five out of uncertainty.
gershom:b4.1: But let them see [in which] category they learned that one; that is, if it was in the category of those three that are of an individual, and they do not know which, let them say three sin offerings die and no more; and if it was among those two that exist in a community, let them say only two sin offerings die.
gershom:b5.1: Rather, they forgot two things: they forgot, so that they did not know which one it is; they forgot [and did not know in which] category. Therefore they established it as five.
gershom:b6.1: And it was difficult for them: If it enters your mind that it was of a community, those others, do they exist in a community? Rather, perforce, the unspecified is learned from the specified, and all of them are said of an individual.
gershom:b7.1: And they do not go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked: unlike consecrated animals whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration and that were redeemed, which are obligated in [the laws of] the firstborn and in the [priestly] gifts, and go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked.
